content.title: Could Timothée Chalamet’s Remarks About Ballet and Opera Cost Him an Oscar? What He Said
content.text: 0 seconds of 0 secondsVolume 0%Loading ad00:2500:0001:47 NEED TO KNOW Timothée Chalamet criticized opera and ballet during a conversation with Matthew McConaughey for Variety and CNN in February 2026He claimed that "no one cares about" the art forms todayChalamet has since faced backlash, leading to speculation that it may cost him an Oscar for his performance in Marty Supreme Timothée Chalamet’s recent remarks about opera and ballet have struck a sour note with the arts community. In February 2026, the actor joined Matthew McConaughey for a Variety and CNN town hall at the University of Texas at Austin, where he made a comment about opera and ballet that some found dismissive. Timothée Chalamet attends the 32nd annual Actor Awards in March 2026. Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic The remark quickly ignited backlash from artists and fans, thrusting Chalamet into the center of a heated public debate. On March 9, the panel on The View weighed in after co-host Sara Haines pointed out that Chalamet’s grandmother, mother and sister all danced with the New York City Ballet. "When you crap on somebody else's art form, it doesn't feel good, it doesn't feel good to see," Whoopi Goldberg added. Related Stories The controversy comes in the final stretch of Chalamet’s Oscar campaign for Marty Supreme. The film earned him nominations for Best Actor and, as a producer, Best Picture. Chalamet has already picked up a Critics Choice Award and a Golden Globe for his performance. So, what did Timothée Chalamet say about ballet and opera? Here's everything to know about the controversy — and if it could cost him an Oscar. What did Timothée Chalamet say about ballet and opera? Matthew McConaughey and Timothée Chalamet during 'Variety' and CNN's town hall in February 2026. Variety/Youtube During the Variety and CNN town hall, Chalamet first reflected on the challenges facing movie theaters in today’s entertainment landscape. "I admire people, and I've done it myself, who go on a talk show and go, 'Hey, we gotta keep movie theaters alive. You know, we gotta keep this genre alive,' " he said. "And another part of me feels like, if people want to see it, like Barbie, like Oppenheimer, they're going to go see it and go out of their way to be loud and proud about it." The conversation eventually turned to other art forms, prompting Chalamet to make an offhanded remark about ballet and opera. "I don't want to be working in ballet or opera, or you know, things where it's like, 'Hey, keep this thing alive,' even though it's like, no one cares about this anymore," he said, drawing laughter from both McConaughey and the crowd. The actor quickly tried to soften the moment, acknowledging how the comment might be perceived. "All respect to the ballet and opera people out there," he added, joking, "I just lost 14 cents in viewership. I just took shots for no reason." How have people responded to Chalamet’s comments? Timothée Chalamet attends the Los Angeles premiere of "Marty Supreme" in December 2025. Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic Chalamet’s remarks triggered a wave of criticism online, as ballet dancers, opera singers, celebrities and major arts institutions pushed back. The Metropolitan Opera shared a TikTok video celebrating its backstage crew with the caption, “This one's for you, @tchalamet.” Meanwhile, the Seattle Opera took a more tongue-in-cheek approach on Instagram. The company offered 14% off select seats for Carmen using the code “TIMOTHEE,” joking in the caption, “Timmy, you're welcome to use it too.” Celebrities have also weighed in. In a since-deleted TikTok post, Doja Cat responded directly to Chalamet’s comments. “Hey, by the way, opera is 400 years old, ballet is 500 years old. Somebody named Tim-oh-tay Cha-lam-et had the nerve — big guy, by the way — had the nerve to say, on camera, that nobody cares about it.” She continued, “I’m sure you can walk into an opera theater right now, seats will be filled out, and nobody’s saying a word as the performance is going because everybody has that much respect for it. People give a f---. You show up in a nice outfit. You sit the f--- down and shut the f--- up. That’s the usual etiquette around those things. Maybe learn something from that," she continued. The principal of Fiorello H. LaGuardia High School — Chalamet’s alma mater — also addressed the controversy in an Instagram statement. “We are so incredibly proud of our own Timothée Chalamet. We cheer for him loudly and with great love. And it is because of that love that I feel compelled to respond to his recent comments about opera and ballet," wrote Deepak Marwah. "At LaGuardia, we do not rank art forms. Timothée, you come from this world. We know your heart, and we know you know better. To every student here studying opera, ballet, or any art the world may tell them 'no one cares about' — we see you. Keep going." Could Chalamet’s remarks cost him an Oscar? Timothée Chalamet in "Marty Supreme"; Timothée Chalamet attends the 83rd annual Golden Globes in January 2026. A24; JC Olivera/2026GG/Penske Media via Getty Despite the backlash, Chalamet’s opera and ballet remarks are unlikely to affect his Oscar prospects. Academy Awards voting officially closed on March 5. While the town hall took place in February 2026, the controversy didn’t gain widespread attention until the day ballots were due — by which point many voters had likely already submitted their picks. But other nominees have moved ahead in many rankings, including Michael B. Jordan, who won Outstanding Performance by a Male Actor in a Leading Role at the March 1 Actor Awards. Jordan has since gained steam in the race, with Gold Derby currently ranking him in first position.
